extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, regulated industry, environmental lawyers, and public commenters on CAA section 111 NSPS rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the Administrator should determine the 'best system of emission reduction' (BSER) and what it means for a system to be 'adequately demonstrated' under Clean Air Act section 111, including considerations of cost, energy, environmental impacts, lead time, subcategories, and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory factors to consider in 'adequately demonstrated' / BSER determination
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(1) and related provisions require the Administrator to take into account cost of compliance, nonair quality health and environmental impact, and energy consideration when determining what is 'adequately demonstrated' and what is the 'best' system of emission reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page quotes statutory language and legislative history emphasizing that these factors are part of the 'adequately demonstrated' determination (e.g., 42 U.S.C. 7419(b)(3); CAA section 111(a)(1)). The preamble and case law (e.g., Sierra Club v. Costle) recognize that EPA may weigh cost, energy, and environmental impacts in deciding what system constitutes the BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability / 'adequately demonstrated' need not require widespread current use
rubrics_metrics.description: A system need only be 'available' or 'could be made available' to be adequately demonstrated; it need not already be broadly used at the time of rule enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and the preamble emphasize Congress intended 'available' or 'could be made available' (House/Senate reports from 1970). EPA has relied on technologies used abroad or only at a single U.S. plant to find adequate demonstration. See examples and citations (e.g., Essex Chem. Corp. v. Ruckelshaus; the 2015 NSPS discussion at 80 FR 64556-58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of projection and extrapolation from testing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may determine a system to be adequately demonstrated based on projections or extrapolation from testing results, rather than requiring a long record of consistent performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited precedent (Sierra Club v. Costle) supports use of short-term testing and extrapolation to identify an appropriate system and standard; the preamble notes EPA may extrapolate from testing results to project performance and thereby identify BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER can be a system-level measure, not strictly limited to measures applied at each source
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'system of emission reduction' is not necessarily confined to control measures that must be applied at and to each individual source; EPA rejected an overly narrow interpretation that would limit BSER to source-level controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ACE Rule's narrow reading (that BSER only includes measures applied at each source) was rejected; EPA may consider broader systems and approaches when identifying BSER (see discussion citing 84 FR 32523-24 and subsequent analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to establish different subcategories for new vs. existing sources
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may establish subcategories based on characteristics relevant to the BSER, and those subcategories can differ between new and existing sources because relevant characteristics may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory citation: 40 CFR 60.22(b)(5), 60.22a(b)(5). The preamble explains that because the definition of subcategories depends on characteristics relevant to the BSER, EPA may set different subcategories for new and existing sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead time to accommodate technology development
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may provide lead time in standards to accommodate development and deployment of projected or emerging technologies relied upon in the BSER determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble states that authorization for lead time accommodates the development of projected technology and references further discussion in section VIII.F of the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness and limits on costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs associated with implementing the BSER must be reasonable — not 'exorbitant' or so great that they exceed what the industry could bear and survive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites case law (e.g., Sierra Club v. Costle; Lignite Energy Council v. EPA; Portland Cement Ass'n v. EPA) and legislative history indicating cost considerations should prevent imposing control costs that the industry could not bear. The preamble treats cost as a balancing factor in setting performance standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferential judicial review of EPA technical judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts apply a deferential standard when reviewing the Administrator's technical judgments in setting standards of performance; decisions will be upheld unless they are arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites judicial standard of review (Nat'l Asphalt Pavement Ass'n v. Train; Ethyl Corp. v. EPA) and explains courts will affirm EPA's actions in highly technical areas absent arbitrary or unreasonable decisionmaking; nevertheless EPA must show reasoned decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional technology‑forcing intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress intended section 111 to be technology‑forcing — encouraging maximum feasible control and allowing EPA to require technologies that may not be widely used yet, subject to reasonable consideration of cost and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites House and Senate reports accompanying the 1970 Clean Air Act emphasizing urgency and the technology‑forcing nature of the statute; this history supports EPA's ability to require ambitious controls that are 'available' or 'could be made available.'
